event.patch_text:
diff --git a/kvstore/evictor.py b/kvstore/evictor.py
index 4ad6598..cf5d3a4 100644
--- a/kvstore/evictor.py
+++ b/kvstore/evictor.py
@@ -1,12 +1,5 @@
 """Background eviction: periodically walks Cache entries and removes ones
 past TTL_SECONDS, so the cache doesn't grow without bound.
-
-Known issue: Cache stores each entry's insertion time in milliseconds
-(Entry.inserted_at_ms), but `now` below is computed in seconds -- so
-`now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is always a large negative number, never
-greater than TTL_SECONDS. The "expired" condition is therefore never true,
-no entry is ever evicted, and the cache grows without bound under
-sustained unique-key traffic.
 """
 
 from __future__ import annotations
@@ -21,11 +14,11 @@ TTL_SECONDS = 300.0
 def run_eviction_pass(cache: Cache) -> int:
     """Remove every entry older than TTL_SECONDS; returns how many were
     removed, so a caller (e.g. a scheduler loop) can log/observe progress."""
-    now = time.time()
+    now_ms = time.time() * 1000
     expired_keys = [
         key
         for key, entry in cache.items()
-        if now - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS
+        if now_ms - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS * 1000
     ]
     for key in expired_keys:
         cache.evict(key)

payload_or_id.title: Expiry rests on an unenforced cross-module unit convention and fails silently
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass converts wall-clock seconds to milliseconds (now_ms = time.time() * 1000, compared against TTL_SECONDS * 1000) to match Entry.inserted_at_ms, which Cache records in milliseconds. Nothing enforces that agreement: the unit is carried only by a field name, the two modules can be changed independently, and a mismatch, a mis-set TTL, or a comparison that can never become true produces no error at all. The pass completes, reports success, and returns 0 -- which is exactly what a healthy pass over an already-clean cache returns. This service shipped precisely that defect (seconds compared against milliseconds) and ran with zero evictions until it was found by reading the code rather than by any signal. The invariant that would make expiry verifiable is that no live entry can be older than TTL_SECONDS; nothing in the service asserts it, exports it, or would notice its breach.

payload_or_id.title: Expiry is driven by wall-clock time, so a clock step expires everything or nothing
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stamps entries with time.time() and run_eviction_pass compares against the same wall clock; neither uses a monotonic source. A backwards step -- NTP correction, VM or container migration, manual adjustment -- shrinks or inverts now_ms - inserted_at_ms and suspends expiry for the duration of the offset, reproducing the never-expires behaviour exactly with no code defect present. A forwards step ages every entry at once, so the next pass evicts the whole cache and drops all traffic into the linear-scan read path. Neither direction raises anything. Because entry age is derived from the same clock, any age-based signal moves with the skew rather than revealing it, which makes this the one eviction failure that the obvious metric cannot see.

payload_or_id.title: Correlated expiry drops a large slice of the cache at once and floods the scan path
payload_or_id.description: TTL is measured from insertion, so entries inserted together expire together: a traffic burst, a warm-up after restart, or any correlated arrival pattern produces a cohort that a single eviction pass removes in one sweep. Every key in that cohort is then a miss on its next request, and each miss costs a full read and linear scan of the backing file. There is no jitter on expiry, no staggered or partial pass, and no refresh-ahead, so occupancy sawtooths and read latency spikes once per pass rather than degrading smoothly. This became reachable only when expiry started working -- before the fix no entry was ever removed, so the cache only ever emptied at a restart.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound whenever expiry stops working
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict has no maximum size and takes an entry for every distinct key requested, including keys that resolved to None. With expiry working, growth is bounded in normal operation by TTL_SECONDS (300): steady state is roughly the number of distinct keys seen within one TTL window, and the entry count should sawtooth rather than climb. It becomes unbounded again the moment expiry stops -- the out-of-repo scheduler is absent or stalled, a clock step suspends the comparison, or the comparison is silently wrong -- and none of those announce themselves. It also exceeds any useful bound when the unique-key arrival rate within one TTL window is high, since the cache has no admission control or replacement policy of its own and cannot bound itself.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked by its out-of-repo scheduler
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function with no loop of its own; an out-of-repo scheduler must call it. If that scheduler was never deployed, is misconfigured, crashed, or silently stopped, the pass simply never runs. With the expiry comparison now correct, this is the largest remaining risk to both the unbounded-growth chain and the staleness chain, because eviction is the only mechanism that bounds cache memory and the only mechanism that ever clears a stale or negative entry. Nothing in the codebase records that a pass ran, so a scheduler that was never deployed, one that stopped an hour ago, and one running normally over a clean cache are indistinguishable from inside the service -- all three produce no signal whatsoever.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass result is discarded, so the eviction path has no health signal
payload_or_id.description: The eviction pass returns the number of entries removed explicitly so a caller can log or observe progress, but nothing in this repo consumes that return value and there is no metric, log line, or timestamp recording that a pass occurred. Two separate questions are therefore unanswerable: whether a pass ran at all, and whether the pass that ran removed what it should have. This is the gap that let the seconds-versus-milliseconds defect run undetected until it was found by reading the code rather than by any operational signal, and it will hide the next eviction failure just as completely -- the one component placed to report on the health of the eviction path throws its own result away.

payload_or_id.title: Absent keys are cached as negative hits that only expiry clears
payload_or_id.description: A storage miss returns None, and Cache.get stores that None as a real Entry. The hit test is `entry is not None`, which tests the Entry wrapper rather than the value, so a cached None is a hit for as long as the entry lives. A key that did not exist when first requested is remembered as absent, and a later write of that key cannot become visible to this process through the normal read path until the entry is removed. No writer invalidates, so expiry is the only thing that ever clears one. Nothing distinguishes a negative entry from a positive one in the cache's own structures, so the share of the cache holding remembered absences is not observable.

payload_or_id.title: Cache never re-checks storage for an already-cached key
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get consults its own dict first and returns immediately on a hit; it never re-checks Storage for an already-cached key and holds no version, checksum, or freshness marker to compare against. There is no read-through revalidation and no TTL check at read time: freshness is enforced entirely out-of-band, by a background pass that removes expired entries between requests. A reader therefore has no way to detect that its cached copy has been superseded, and no way to notice that the pass which is supposed to bound its staleness has stopped running.

payload_or_id.title: Cache is process-local with no cross-instance invalidation
payload_or_id.description: The cache lives in a plain process-local dict with no sharing, no invalidation broadcast, and no coordination between instances. Any two processes serving reads diverge as soon as a write occurs, since each holds whatever it cached at whatever moment it first saw the key. Expiry now bounds how long that divergence persists -- each instance independently discards entries older than TTL_SECONDS (300) -- but nothing makes them converge any sooner, and the bound is per instance: one process whose eviction has stopped stays out of step with the rest indefinitely while every other instance looks healthy.

payload_or_id.title: Clients are served a superseded value for up to a full TTL after a write
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value for a key that is already cached and receives the value from before the most recent write. The write path does not invalidate the entry and the read path does not revalidate, so the only thing that ever reconciles them is expiry: the staleness window is TTL_SECONDS (300), not the remaining lifetime of the process. That bounded window is the designed behaviour, which is why this is a warning rather than a page -- but it holds only while eviction actually runs, and every way eviction can stop is silent, at which point the window reverts to unbounded. The call returns normally and increments outcome="success", and nothing distinguishes a stale read from a correct one at any layer, so the bound is the only protection clients have.

payload_or_id.title: A key written after its first lookup stays invisible to clients for a full TTL
payload_or_id.description: A client asks for a key that does not exist yet, and the miss is cached as a negative entry. The sync job later writes that key successfully. Every subsequent read from this process still returns None until that entry is removed, because the negative entry is a cache hit and no writer invalidates it. Expiry now clears it after TTL_SECONDS (300), so the key becomes visible within one TTL of being written rather than never for the life of the process. It reverts to permanent invisibility on any instance whose eviction has stopped, and while it lasts it is worse than ordinary staleness: the client sees the key as absent rather than out of date, and a caller that treats absence as authoritative will act on it.

payload_or_id.title: Identical requests return different values depending on which instance serves them
payload_or_id.description: With more than one process serving reads, each holds its own independent cache populated at whatever moment it first saw each key. After a write, instances that had the key cached keep the old value while instances that did not return the new one. A client retrying a request, or two clients reading concurrently, get different answers with no pattern they can detect or route around. Expiry bounds the divergence to roughly one TTL_SECONDS window (300) per key rather than the lifetime of the processes, so caches converge instead of drifting apart permanently -- but only for instances whose eviction pass is actually running, and no signal compares instances against one another, so a single lagging instance is invisible.

payload_or_id.title: Every key reads as absent after data loss or a lost backing file
payload_or_id.description: Total or partial data loss -- a truncated file from an interrupted rewrite, a deleted file, an unmounted volume, a wrong path -- presents to clients as every key returning None. Storage raises nothing for a missing path and the API counts each call as outcome="success", so a complete data-loss incident produces a perfectly green error rate. Each empty result is also cached as a negative entry, so the outage outlives its own repair: after the file is restored clients keep being served absences until those entries expire, up to a full TTL_SECONDS (300) later, and indefinitely on any instance whose eviction pass has stopped.

payload_or_id.title: Process is killed by memory exhaustion and reads fail outright
payload_or_id.description: The cache exhausts the process or container memory limit and the process is OOM-killed, dropping in-flight requests and making the service unavailable until it restarts. Restart empties the cache, so the service recovers and climbs back toward the same ceiling: the signature is a sawtooth crash-loop whose period shortens as traffic grows. Working expiry makes this reachable only when eviction has stopped or when the unique-key rate within one TTL window holds an oversized working set, since the cache still imposes no limit of its own. Each restart also erases the counters, and the cold cache that follows drives a miss storm into the linear-scan read path, so recovery is at its slowest exactly when load is at its heaviest.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the backing file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads and scans the entire backing file, so per-request latency grows linearly with the stored key count. Clients see gradually rising response times, punctuated by sharp spikes whenever a large share of the cache turns over at once: after every restart, when the cold cache turns all traffic into misses, and now also after an eviction pass sweeps out a cohort of entries that were inserted together. Nothing measures latency or the hit ratio, so the degradation is only ever noticed downstream in a client's own timeouts.

There is no jitter on expiry, no staggered or partial pass, and no refresh-ahead, so occupancy sawtooths and read latency spikes once per pass rather than degrading smoothly. This became reachable only when expiry started working -- before the fix no entry was ever removed, so the cache only ever emptied at a restart.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound whenever expiry stops working
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict has no maximum size and takes an entry for every distinct key requested, including keys that resolved to None. With expiry working, growth is bounded in normal operation by TTL_SECONDS (300): steady state is roughly the number of distinct keys seen within one TTL window, and the entry count should sawtooth rather than climb. It becomes unbounded again the moment expiry stops -- the out-of-repo scheduler is absent or stalled, a clock step suspends the comparison, or the comparison is silently wrong -- and none of those announce themselves. It also exceeds any useful bound when the unique-key arrival rate within one TTL window is high, since the cache has no admission control or replacement policy of its own and cannot bound itself.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked by its out-of-repo scheduler
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function with no loop of its own; an out-of-repo scheduler must call it. If that scheduler was never deployed, is misconfigured, crashed, or silently stopped, the pass simply never runs. With the expiry comparison now correct, this is the largest remaining risk to both the unbounded-growth chain and the staleness chain, because eviction is the only mechanism that bounds cache memory and the only mechanism that ever clears a stale or negative entry. Nothing in the codebase records that a pass ran, so a scheduler that was never deployed, one that stopped an hour ago, and one running normally over a clean cache are indistinguishable from inside the service -- all three produce no signal whatsoever.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass result is discarded, so the eviction path has no health signal
payload_or_id.description: The eviction pass returns the number of entries removed explicitly so a caller can log or observe progress, but nothing in this repo consumes that return value and there is no metric, log line, or timestamp recording that a pass occurred. Two separate questions are therefore unanswerable: whether a pass ran at all, and whether the pass that ran removed what it should have. This is the gap that let the seconds-versus-milliseconds defect run undetected until it was found by reading the code rather than by any operational signal, and it will hide the next eviction failure just as completely -- the one component placed to report on the health of the eviction path throws its own result away.

payload_or_id.title: Absent keys are cached as negative hits that only expiry clears
payload_or_id.description: A storage miss returns None, and Cache.get stores that None as a real Entry. The hit test is `entry is not None`, which tests the Entry wrapper rather than the value, so a cached None is a hit for as long as the entry lives. A key that did not exist when first requested is remembered as absent, and a later write of that key cannot become visible to this process through the normal read path until the entry is removed. No writer invalidates, so expiry is the only thing that ever clears one. Nothing distinguishes a negative entry from a positive one in the cache's own structures, so the share of the cache holding remembered absences is not observable.

payload_or_id.title: Cache never re-checks storage for an already-cached key
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get consults its own dict first and returns immediately on a hit; it never re-checks Storage for an already-cached key and holds no version, checksum, or freshness marker to compare against. There is no read-through revalidation and no TTL check at read time: freshness is enforced entirely out-of-band, by a background pass that removes expired entries between requests. A reader therefore has no way to detect that its cached copy has been superseded, and no way to notice that the pass which is supposed to bound its staleness has stopped running.

payload_or_id.title: Cache is process-local with no cross-instance invalidation
payload_or_id.description: The cache lives in a plain process-local dict with no sharing, no invalidation broadcast, and no coordination between instances. Any two processes serving reads diverge as soon as a write occurs, since each holds whatever it cached at whatever moment it first saw the key. Expiry now bounds how long that divergence persists -- each instance independently discards entries older than TTL_SECONDS (300) -- but nothing makes them converge any sooner, and the bound is per instance: one process whose eviction has stopped stays out of step with the rest indefinitely while every other instance looks healthy.

payload_or_id.title: Clients are served a superseded value for up to a full TTL after a write
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value for a key that is already cached and receives the value from before the most recent write. The write path does not invalidate the entry and the read path does not revalidate, so the only thing that ever reconciles them is expiry: the staleness window is TTL_SECONDS (300), not the remaining lifetime of the process. That bounded window is the designed behaviour, which is why this is a warning rather than a page -- but it holds only while eviction actually runs, and every way eviction can stop is silent, at which point the window reverts to unbounded. The call returns normally and increments outcome="success", and nothing distinguishes a stale read from a correct one at any layer, so the bound is the only protection clients have.

payload_or_id.title: A key written after its first lookup stays invisible to clients for a full TTL
payload_or_id.description: A client asks for a key that does not exist yet, and the miss is cached as a negative entry. The sync job later writes that key successfully. Every subsequent read from this process still returns None until that entry is removed, because the negative entry is a cache hit and no writer invalidates it. Expiry now clears it after TTL_SECONDS (300), so the key becomes visible within one TTL of being written rather than never for the life of the process. It reverts to permanent invisibility on any instance whose eviction has stopped, and while it lasts it is worse than ordinary staleness: the client sees the key as absent rather than out of date, and a caller that treats absence as authoritative will act on it.

payload_or_id.title: Identical requests return different values depending on which instance serves them
payload_or_id.description: With more than one process serving reads, each holds its own independent cache populated at whatever moment it first saw each key. After a write, instances that had the key cached keep the old value while instances that did not return the new one. A client retrying a request, or two clients reading concurrently, get different answers with no pattern they can detect or route around. Expiry bounds the divergence to roughly one TTL_SECONDS window (300) per key rather than the lifetime of the processes, so caches converge instead of drifting apart permanently -- but only for instances whose eviction pass is actually running, and no signal compares instances against one another, so a single lagging instance is invisible.

payload_or_id.title: Every key reads as absent after data loss or a lost backing file
payload_or_id.description: Total or partial data loss -- a truncated file from an interrupted rewrite, a deleted file, an unmounted volume, a wrong path -- presents to clients as every key returning None. Storage raises nothing for a missing path and the API counts each call as outcome="success", so a complete data-loss incident produces a perfectly green error rate. Each empty result is also cached as a negative entry, so the outage outlives its own repair: after the file is restored clients keep being served absences until those entries expire, up to a full TTL_SECONDS (300) later, and indefinitely on any instance whose eviction pass has stopped.

payload_or_id.title: Process is killed by memory exhaustion and reads fail outright
payload_or_id.description: The cache exhausts the process or container memory limit and the process is OOM-killed, dropping in-flight requests and making the service unavailable until it restarts. Restart empties the cache, so the service recovers and climbs back toward the same ceiling: the signature is a sawtooth crash-loop whose period shortens as traffic grows. Working expiry makes this reachable only when eviction has stopped or when the unique-key rate within one TTL window holds an oversized working set, since the cache still imposes no limit of its own. Each restart also erases the counters, and the cold cache that follows drives a miss storm into the linear-scan read path, so recovery is at its slowest exactly when load is at its heaviest.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the backing file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads and scans the entire backing file, so per-request latency grows linearly with the stored key count. Clients see gradually rising response times, punctuated by sharp spikes whenever a large share of the cache turns over at once: after every restart, when the cold cache turns all traffic into misses, and now also after an eviction pass sweeps out a cohort of entries that were inserted together. Nothing measures latency or the hit ratio, so the degradation is only ever noticed downstream in a client's own timeouts.

One signal therefore covers a scheduler that never runs and an expiry comparison that silently never becomes true, without needing to distinguish them. That second case is not hypothetical: the service shipped a seconds-versus-milliseconds comparison that evicted nothing and produced no signal at all, and this gauge is what would have shown it within one TTL. annotations.summary: kvstore eviction removed more than half the cache in a single sweep
annotations.description: One eviction pass has discarded over half of the cached entries. TTL is measured from insertion, so entries that arrived together expire together: a traffic burst, a warm-up after a restart, or any correlated arrival pattern produces a cohort that a single pass removes in one sweep. Every key in that cohort is a miss on its next request, and each miss costs a full read and linear scan of the backing file, so this rule fires ahead of the latency spike it predicts rather than after it. There is no jitter on expiry, no staggered or partial pass, and no refresh-ahead, so the condition recurs on a period set by the traffic pattern rather than resolving on its own. Confirm with KvstoreReadLatencyHigh on source="storage_read" and with the cache entry count, which will show the matching vertical drop. A single very large sweep with no matching traffic burst behind it may instead be a forwards clock step -- check KvstoreClockSkew. Remedies are jittered TTLs, partial passes, or refresh-ahead; none exist today.

annotations.summary: kvstore process clock disagrees with the monitoring server by over 30 seconds
annotations.description: Cache.get stamps entries with time.time() and run_eviction_pass compares against the same wall clock, with no monotonic source anywhere in the expiry path, so a clock step silently redefines what "expired" means with no code defect present. A backwards step shrinks or inverts the age difference and suspends expiry for the duration of the offset, reproducing the never-expires behaviour exactly; a forwards step ages every entry at once so the next pass evicts the whole cache. This rule exists for attribution rather than detection: the consequences already surface as KvstoreCacheEvictionIneffective or KvstoreCacheEvictionMassSweep, but neither can tell a stepped clock from a broken comparison, and the two need completely different remedies. The oldest-entry-age gauge cannot help either, since it derives age from the same clock it would need to audit -- which is why this rule compares against Prometheus's own clock instead. The 30s threshold is a placeholder: it must sit well above scrape and network jitter and well below TTL_SECONDS (300), since skew approaching a full TTL is what makes expiry behave arbitrarily. Prefer node_exporter's node_timex_offset_seconds and node_timex_sync_status if those are already scraped for these hosts. The durable fix is to measure entry age on a monotonic clock.

annotations.summary: Over a quarter of kvstore cache entries are cached absences
annotations.description: The cache is accumulating None-valued entries. Because the hit test checks the Entry wrapper rather than the value, a cached None is a hit for as long as the entry lives: a key first requested before it was written stays invisible to this process however many times the sync job writes it, since no writer invalidates. Expiry now bounds that invisibility to TTL_SECONDS (300) rather than the lifetime of the process, which is why this is a ticket rather than a page -- but a quarter of the cache spent on remembered absences sustained over half an hour means keys are being requested well before they exist, and on any instance whose eviction pass has stopped the condition does not clear at all. A sharp step up is also an early signature of the backing file having gone missing or been truncated, so rule that out with KvstoreBackingFileMissing and KvstoreStorageKeysDropped before treating this as a client access-pattern problem.

annotations.summary: kvstore backing file does not exist -- every key reads as absent
annotations.description: The backing file is gone: deleted, on an unmounted volume, or behind a path that changed. Storage.get returns None without raising for a missing path, so every read reports outcome="success" and the service looks perfectly healthy while serving nothing. The short 2m window is deliberate -- this is total data unavailability with a completely green error rate, and every minute it persists also fills the cache with negative entries that outlive the repair. Restoring the file does not restore service immediately: clients keep being served absences until those entries expire, up to a full TTL_SECONDS (300) later, and indefinitely on any instance whose eviction pass has stopped, which still needs a restart to clear them.

annotations.summary: Over half of kvstore reads are returning absent
annotations.description: Most requests are resolving to no value. This is the client-visible end of the data-loss chain and it is invisible to the metric as instrumented today, where every one of these calls increments outcome="success" -- which is precisely why the result label was recommended. Distinguishes total unavailability (paired with KvstoreBackingFileMissing or KvstoreStorageKeysDropped) from cached negative entries (paired with KvstoreNegativeCacheEntriesHigh), which now clear within one TTL_SECONDS window once the underlying data is back rather than persisting for the life of the process. Treat a sudden step change as data loss until proven otherwise; a surge that decays over roughly a TTL after a storage problem was fixed is the cache draining its remembered absences.

annotations.summary: One or more recommended kvstore metrics are not being reported
annotations.description: A metric this alerting set depends on is missing. These failure modes are themselves instrumentation gaps -- the write path, the eviction pass, and the read path emit nothing, and the request counter lacks the labels that would separate correct reads from stale ones -- so the alert for each is necessarily a check that the fix exists and has not regressed. annotations.summary: kvstore process memory is projected to exhaust its limit within six hours
annotations.description: Resident memory is trending toward the configured limit, most likely driven by the cache -- which has no size limit of its own and stays bounded only while the eviction pass keeps running. predict_linear is used rather than a static threshold because growth here is steady and predictable, which buys hours of warning instead of minutes, and because the OOM kill destroys its own evidence, resetting every application counter and clearing the cache, so post-hoc diagnosis is unreliable. process_resident_memory_bytes comes from the default process collectors enabled by the exposition recommendation, not from application code; correlate with kvstore_cache_entries to confirm the cache is the driver, and with KvstoreCacheEvictionStalled and KvstoreCacheEvictionIneffective to find out whether expiry has stopped or the working set within one TTL window is simply too large. The 2e9 threshold is a placeholder: set it to roughly 85% of the actual container or cgroup memory limit for this deployment.

payload_or_id.title: Expiry rests on an unenforced cross-module unit convention and fails silently
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass converts wall-clock seconds to milliseconds (now_ms = time.time() * 1000, compared against TTL_SECONDS * 1000) to match Entry.inserted_at_ms, which Cache records in milliseconds. Nothing enforces that agreement: the unit is carried only by a field name, the two modules can be changed independently, and a mismatch, a mis-set TTL, or a comparison that can never become true produces no error at all. The pass completes, reports success, and returns 0 -- which is exactly what a healthy pass over an already-clean cache returns. This service shipped precisely that defect (seconds compared against milliseconds) and ran with zero evictions until it was found by reading the code rather than by any signal. The invariant that would make expiry verifiable is that no live entry can be older than TTL_SECONDS; nothing in the service asserts it, exports it, or would notice its breach.

payload_or_id.title: Expiry is driven by wall-clock time, so a clock step expires everything or nothing
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stamps entries with time.time() and run_eviction_pass compares against the same wall clock; neither uses a monotonic source. A backwards step -- NTP correction, VM or container migration, manual adjustment -- shrinks or inverts now_ms - inserted_at_ms and suspends expiry for the duration of the offset, reproducing the never-expires behaviour exactly with no code defect present. A forwards step ages every entry at once, so the next pass evicts the whole cache and drops all traffic into the linear-scan read path. Neither direction raises anything. Because entry age is derived from the same clock, any age-based signal moves with the skew rather than revealing it, which makes this the one eviction failure that the obvious metric cannot see: detecting it needs an independent time source, which is why it is covered by comparing the process's wall clock against the monitoring server's rather than by the oldest-entry-age gauge.

payload_or_id.title: Correlated expiry drops a large slice of the cache at once and floods the scan path

There is no jitter on expiry, no staggered or partial pass, and no refresh-ahead, so occupancy sawtooths and read latency spikes once per pass rather than degrading smoothly. This became reachable only when expiry started working -- before the fix no entry was ever removed, so the cache only ever emptied at a restart.
